title: Copies of true love
sum: Polycarp and the elders of Smyrna greet the church at Philippi, a church that 'lives as a resident alien' in its city (1:0). He rejoices that the Philippians welcomed prisoners in chains, 'the copies of true love', on their way to death in Rome (1:1), and that their faith, famous since Paul's day, still bears fruit (1:2). Then, in words borrowed from 1 Peter and Ephesians, he names the root of that faith: Christ who died and was raised, the unseen Lord they love with 'a joy that words cannot tell', and the grace that saves 'not from works' (1:3).
The chapter sets the tone of the letter: warm, humble, made almost entirely of the language of the apostles. Polycarp claims no title for himself, and he greets a church he admires.

views.H: The prisoners of 1:1 are named in 9:1, Ignatius, Zosimus and Rufus. Eusebius tells of Ignatius's journey from Syria through Asia to Rome (Church History 3.36.3-10), and Ignatius's own letter to Polycarp says he would sail from Troas to Neapolis, Philippi's port (To Polycarp 8). That ties the letter to a real journey, though the year is debated (see chapter 13).
views.N: Three New Testament books shape these lines: Acts 2:24 ('untying the birth pains'), 1 Peter 1:8 ('a joy that words cannot tell, a joy made glorious') and Ephesians 2:8-9 ('by grace ... not from works'). Polycarp quotes without saying he is quoting; the words are simply his.
views.C: Polycarp praises the Philippians' escort of the prisoners as love, as 3 John 6 praises sending travelers on their way 'in a way worthy of God'.

deep.h: Grace, works and the shape of the letter
deep.b: Polycarp says the Philippians are saved 'by grace ... not from works' (1:3), and then spends most of the letter on works: serve God, keep away from love of money, forgive, care for widows and the sick. He sees no conflict. The grace comes first, and the life follows it, as in Ephesians 2:8-10, where Paul's 'not from works' is followed by 'created in Christ Jesus for good works'. His resurrection promise in 2:2 has a condition, 'if we do his will', and the churches have read such pairings in different ways; the site's cards at Ephesians 2, Romans 3 and James 2 give the views.

echoes: Acts 2:24; 1 Peter 1:8; Ephesians 2:5; Ephesians 2:8-9; 1 Peter 1:17; Jude 2; Revelation 2:10

settings.what: The greeting and thanksgiving of the letter
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: After prisoners, Ignatius among them, had passed through Philippi on the way to Rome, and the Philippians had written to Smyrna (13:1-2)
settings.why: To honor the Philippians' care for the prisoners and their long faith, and to set out at the start the gospel on which every later instruction rests: Christ's death and resurrection, and salvation by grace. Knowing that the letter answers a request (3:1) makes the praise a real reply, not a formula.

title: What the Lord said when he taught
sum: 'So tuck up your robes and serve God' (2:1). Polycarp grounds his teaching in Christ's exaltation: raised, enthroned, ruler of all things in heaven and on earth, coming as judge (2:1). The God who raised him will raise us too, if we walk in his commands and keep away from greed, slander and revenge (2:2). Then he gives the Lord's own words: 'Do not judge ... Forgive ... Show mercy', and two beatitudes joined into one (2:3).
The sayings of 2:3 are close to Matthew and Luke but match neither exactly, and 1 Clement 13:2 gives two of the same lines. They bear on the question of how Jesus' words were handed on.

views.N: Polycarp's saying list mixes Matthew 7:1-2 (exact Greek in the first line), Luke 6:36-38 (the measure), and lines found in no Gospel in this form but also in 1 Clement 13:2. The texts show two letters drawing on a shared set of sayings; they do not show whether that set was oral, a written collection, or the Gospels remembered loosely.
views.C: The list of sins in 2:2 (unrighteousness, greed, love of money, slander, false testimony) previews the trouble at Philippi, where an elder fell through greed (11:1). The cure Polycarp offers is the Lord's teaching on judging and forgiving, which he applies directly to that case in 11:4.

readings: Christ raised and coming (2:1), our resurrection and how to live for it (2:2), the Lord's words as the rule (2:3): the pattern of much early Christian teaching, belief first and then conduct.
Set 2:3 beside Matthew 7:1-2 and Luke 6:36-38 and the overlaps and differences are plain. Polycarp is a witness to the words of Jesus as one Christian of Asia remembered and used them.
echoes: Psalm 2:11; 1 Peter 1:13; 1 Peter 1:21; Philippians 2:10; Philippians 3:21; Acts 10:42; 2 Corinthians 4:14; 1 Peter 3:9; Matthew 7:1-2; Luke 6:20; Luke 6:36-38; Matthew 5:3; Matthew 5:10; 1 Clement 13:2

settings.what: Teaching: serve God, who raised Christ and will raise us
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: Early in the letter, before the instructions for each group in the church
settings.why: To give the reason for everything that follows: the risen Christ will judge, and the God who raised him will raise those who do his will.

settings.what: Words of the Lord Jesus, quoted by Polycarp
settings.by: Jesus, as Polycarp remembers his teaching
settings.to: Jesus' disciples and the crowds in the Gospels; here, the church at Philippi
settings.when: Quoted as 'what the Lord said when he taught'
settings.why: To set the Lord's own words against revenge and harsh judgment, in a church that had to deal with a fallen elder (11:4). The letter does not say why the sayings against judging come first; one reading is that the Philippians would have to judge the case of Valens.
settings.readers: The church at Philippi in Macedonia, founded by Paul, which had just welcomed Ignatius and other prisoners on their way to Rome (1:1; 9:1), had written to Polycarp asking for a word of teaching, a carrier for its letter to Syria and copies of Ignatius's letters (3:1; 13:1-2), and was troubled by the fall of one of its elders (11:1-4).

title: The wisdom of Paul
sum: Polycarp writes about righteousness only because the Philippians asked (3:1). Neither he nor anyone like him can keep up with 'the blessed and glorious Paul', who taught them in person and wrote them letters (3:2). Study those letters and grow in faith, 'the mother of us all', with hope behind and love ahead; whoever has love has fulfilled the command (3:3).
The chapter shows how a leader of the next generation saw Paul: not a rival, but the teacher whose letters the church should read and reread.

views.H: The plural 'letters' (3:2) has puzzled readers, since the New Testament has one letter to the Philippians, and the Latin of 11:3 has 'his letter'. The texts allow several explanations; none is proved (see the note).
views.N: Polycarp turns Galatians 4:26's 'mother of us all', in the wording of the Byzantine text, into a description of faith, and orders faith, hope and love (1 Corinthians 13:13) into a procession. He reads Paul as a whole, moving from one letter to another.

settings.what: Polycarp explains why he writes, and points to Paul
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: In answer to the Philippians' request to write to them 'about righteousness' (3:1)
settings.why: To decline any claim to authority of his own and send the Philippians back to Paul's teaching. Knowing that Philippi had been taught and written to by Paul makes his modesty pointed: they already have better teaching than his.

title: The beginning of every trouble
sum: 'Love of money is where every trouble begins' (4:1), in words from 1 Timothy 6. So the leaders must first arm themselves with righteousness, then teach their wives to love their husbands and raise their children in the fear of God (4:2), and the widows to pray for everyone, to keep away from slander and greed, and to know that they are 'God's altar', where everything offered is checked for blemishes (4:3).
This begins a code of duties for each group in the church (4:2-6:3), like the household codes of the New Testament but centered on church groups.

views.N: 1 Timothy 6:7 and 6:10 are quoted with small changes, and 1 Timothy 5:5 stands behind the praying widows. Polycarp uses the Pastoral Letters often (4:1; 5:2; 9:2; 11:4; 12:3).
views.C: The widows in 4:3 are a recognized group, supported by the church and expected to pray; 1 Timothy 5:3-16 sets rules for such a group. Calling them 'God's altar' gives them a place of honor in the church's worship, and the image recurs in later Christian writings (see the note).

echoes: 1 Timothy 6:7; 1 Timothy 6:10; 2 Corinthians 6:7; 1 Timothy 5:5; 1 Corinthians 14:25; Ephesians 5:22-6:4

settings.what: Instructions: the love of money, wives and widows
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: The first part of the code of duties for groups in the church
settings.why: To name the root problem, love of money, before anything else, and to give each group its part. Read with chapter 11, the warning is aimed at the trouble Philippi was living through.

title: Deacons, young men and virgins
sum: 'God is not sneered at' (5:1). Deacons must be blameless, truthful, free of the love of money, living by the truth of the Lord, 'who became the servant of all' (5:2). The younger men must keep themselves pure, for desires war against the Spirit, and Paul's list of those who will not inherit the kingdom applies to them (5:3). All must submit to the elders and deacons 'as to God and Christ', and the virgins must keep a pure conscience (5:3).
Deacons appear here as a known office; elders come in chapter 6. An overseer is never mentioned.

views.N: Galatians 6:7 (5:1), 1 Timothy 3:8 (the deacons' qualities), Philippians 1:27 ('live as citizens worthy'), 2 Timothy 2:12 ('we will also reign with him'), 1 Peter 2:11 and Galatians 5:17 (the war of desire), 1 Corinthians 6:9-10. The chapter is a patchwork of Paul and Peter.
views.C: Polycarp's church has deacons and elders whom the people are to obey 'as God and Christ', a phrase close to Ignatius's (To the Smyrnaeans 8), but unlike Ignatius he names no overseer. How the offices of overseer and elder relate is a point on which today's churches differ; the site's cards at Philippians 1, 1 Timothy 3 and Acts 20 give the views.

echoes: Galatians 6:7; 1 Timothy 3:8-13; Mark 9:35; Philippians 1:27; 2 Timothy 2:12; 1 Peter 2:11; Galatians 5:17; 1 Corinthians 6:9-10; 1 Peter 5:5

settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: The middle of the code of duties
settings.why: To hold the church's servants and its young people to the standard of Christ the servant, and to keep the church under its leaders while one of those leaders had failed (11:1).

title: Elders who forgive
sum: The elders must be tenderhearted shepherds: bring back the strays, visit the sick, care for widows, orphans and the poor, avoid anger, favoritism and love of money, and be slow to believe a charge, because 'we all owe a debt of sin' (6:1). Whoever asks forgiveness must forgive, since all will stand before Christ's judgment seat (6:2). So let us serve him with fear, as he and the apostles and prophets taught, and keep away from false brothers and hypocrites (6:3).
The instructions to the elders come last, and they are the most detailed. Polycarp's picture of an elder is a pastor, not a ruler.

views.N: Ezekiel 34 and James 1:27 stand behind the elders' duties, 2 Corinthians 8:21 (Proverbs 3:4 in Greek) behind 'plan ahead for what is good', and Romans 14:10-12 with 2 Corinthians 5:10 behind the judgment seat.
views.C: 'They must not be quick to believe a charge against anyone, or be harsh when they judge' (6:1) is advice for the case of Valens (11:1-4): the elders who must deal with a fallen colleague must judge gently, knowing their own debt of sin. Pope Leo XIV quotes the opening of 6:1, on the elders' care for widows, orphans and the poor, in his 2025 exhortation Dilexi te (paragraph 39).

echoes: Ezekiel 34:4; Ezekiel 34:16; James 1:27; 2 Corinthians 8:21; Matthew 6:12; Romans 14:10-12; 2 Corinthians 5:10; Psalm 2:11; Hebrews 12:28; 2 Peter 3:2; Galatians 2:4

settings.what: Instructions: the elders, and all the church
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: The end of the code of duties
settings.why: To describe the elders' work as care for the weak and forgiveness, and to warn the whole church away from hypocrites. Since the church's crisis concerned an elder, this section speaks to the men who would judge him.

title: The firstborn of Satan
sum: Polycarp's sharpest words: 'everyone who does not confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is an antichrist'; whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is from the devil; and whoever bends the Lord's sayings to his own desires and denies resurrection and judgment is 'the firstborn of Satan' (7:1). So turn back to the word handed down from the beginning, pray, fast, and ask God not to bring us into testing, for 'The spirit is eager, the flesh weak' (7:2).

The chapter names no teacher. It joins 1 John's test of the true Christ to a warning against those who deny the resurrection, and it answers both with prayer and with the tradition received from the start.

views.H: Irenaeus says Polycarp once called Marcion 'the first-born of Satan' (Against Heresies 3.3.4). P. N. Harrison took 7:1 as aimed at Marcion and dated chapters 1-12 accordingly; C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd, and Lightfoot as the Catholic Encyclopedia reports him, denied it. See the deep section.
views.N: 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 7 (the antichrist), 1 Corinthians 15:12 and 2 Timothy 2:18 (the resurrection denied), 1 John 2:24 and Jude 3 (the word from the beginning), 1 Peter 4:7 (prayer), Matthew 6:13 and 26:41 (the Lord's Prayer and Gethsemane).
views.C: The answer to false teaching is not a debate but a return: to the word handed down at first, and to prayer and fasting. How tradition and Scripture relate is a point where the churches differ (topic Scripture and tradition).

deep.b: Polycarp describes three marks: they deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, they do not confess 'the testimony of the cross', and they twist the Lord's sayings to deny resurrection and judgment. The first two match the teachers Ignatius fought at Smyrna, who said Christ 'only seemed to suffer' (To the Smyrnaeans 2, ANF). Later Christians called this view docetism, from Greek dokeō, 'seem'. The third may be the same people or others; Paul met resurrection-deniers at Corinth (1 Corinthians 15:12).

Irenaeus, who heard Polycarp as a boy (Eusebius, Church History 5.20.5-6), tells that when Marcion met him and said 'Do you know me?', Polycarp answered, 'I do know you, the first-born of Satan' (Against Heresies 3.3.4, ANF). Lake's footnote at 7:1 says the phrase 'was applied, presumably later, by Polycarp to Marcion'. P. N. Harrison (1936) argued that the letter already meant Marcion, which would date chapters 1-12 to the 130s; Carl Schneider (1937) agreed. C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd, who accepted Harrison's two letters, denied 'any reference to Marcion' (so Harrison's reply of 1948, which names all three). The Catholic Encyclopedia says Harnack came to admit that 'there need be no reference to Marcion at all', and gives Lightfoot's reasons: 'nothing is said about his characteristic errors, e.g., the distinction between the God of the Old and the God of the New Testament', and 'the antinomianism ascribed to "the first-born of Satan" is inapplicable to the austere Marcion'. Irenaeus's story shows at least that the phrase was one Polycarp used.

echoes: 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7; 1 John 3:8; 1 Corinthians 15:12; 2 Timothy 2:18; 1 John 2:24; Jude 3; 1 Peter 4:7; Matthew 6:13; Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38

settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: After the duties of each group; the false teachers of 6:3 are now described
settings.why: To mark off the church from teaching that denied Christ's real body, death and resurrection, and to send the church back to its first teaching and to prayer. The Philippians are not said to have accepted such teaching; the warning protects them.

title: The model to trace
sum: Hold on to our hope, Christ Jesus, the down payment of our righteousness, who 'carried our sins up in his own body onto the tree' and 'did no sin' (8:1, from 1 Peter 2:22-24). So imitate his endurance, and if we suffer for his name, give him glory: he is the model we trace (8:2).
The chapter turns the letter toward suffering, preparing for the examples of the martyrs in chapter 9.

views.N: 1 Peter 2:21-24 governs the whole chapter: the quotation from Isaiah 53 by way of 1 Peter (8:1), and 1 Peter's own word hypogrammos, the 'model to trace' (8:2). Eusebius's remark that Polycarp used 'testimonies' from 1 Peter fits it well (Church History 4.14.9).
views.C: Imitation of Christ in suffering is the thread that runs from this letter into the Martyrdom of Polycarp, which tells Polycarp's own death as a martyrdom 'in line with the gospel' (Martyrdom of Polycarp 1:1).

echoes: 1 Peter 2:21-24; Isaiah 53:9; Isaiah 53:12; Ephesians 1:14; 1 Timothy 1:1; 1 Peter 4:16

settings.what: Exhortation: hold on to Christ and imitate his endurance
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: As the letter turns from duties to suffering
settings.why: To give the Philippians, who had seen prisoners led to death (1:1; 9:1), the reason to stand firm if their turn came: Christ endured for them, and they are to trace his pattern.

title: They did not run for nothing
sum: Practice endurance, Polycarp urges, the endurance you saw 'right in front of you' in Ignatius, Zosimus and Rufus, in others from your own church, and in Paul and the apostles (9:1). None of them ran for nothing: they are in the place owed to them, with the Lord with whom they suffered, because they loved him, not 'the present age' (9:2).
Here the Greek manuscripts end, in the middle of 9:2. Eusebius quotes both verses, and from 10:1 to 12:3 only the Latin remains.

views.H: If Ignatius is already 'with the Lord' here, but in 13:2 Polycarp asks for news of him, the letter may join two letters written at different times (Harrison's view) or speak in 9:2 of a death taken as certain (the view of the Catholic Encyclopedia). See chapter 13.
views.N: Philippians 2:16 ('did not run for nothing'), 2 Timothy 4:10 ('the present age') and 1 Clement 5:4 ('the place owed' to Peter) supply the wording.
views.C: Polycarp sets recent martyrs beside Paul and the apostles as examples for a church. The honor given to martyrs, which the Martyrdom of Polycarp develops (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:3; 18:3), starts here as simple remembrance.

deep.b: Chapter 9 speaks of Ignatius as already 'in the place owed to them, with the Lord'. Chapter 13 asks the Philippians for anything certain about 'Ignatius himself and those who are with him'. In 1936 P. N. Harrison (Polycarp's Two Epistles to the Philippians) proposed that our letter joins two: a short 'Covering Note' (chapter 13), sent with Ignatius's letters while he was still on the road, and a later 'Crisis Letter' (chapters 1-12) about Valens and the false teachers, which he dated about 135-137. His reply of 1948 names C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd as agreeing on two letters, 'one before, the other after, the death of Ignatius', but putting the second 'only a few months, or at most a year or two, after the first'. On the one-letter reading of the Catholic Encyclopedia, Polycarp 'wrote his epistle before he had heard of St. Ignatius' martyrdom', so 9:2 counts the condemned Ignatius among the martyrs while 13:2 asks for firm news. Lake's introduction treats the letter as one 'covering letter'.

settings.what: Exhortation: the example of the martyrs
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: While the memory of the prisoners' visit was fresh (1:1)
settings.why: To turn the Philippians' own memories, of Ignatius's chains and of Paul's beating in their city, into a call to endure.

title: Alms rescue from death
sum: From here the Plain English Translation follows the old Latin translation, because Polycarp's Greek is lost. Stand firm, follow the Lord's pattern, love one another, look down on no one (10:1). Do good without delay, 'because alms rescue from death'; submit to one another; live blamelessly among the Gentiles so that the Lord's name is not insulted (10:2). Woe to anyone through whom it is (10:3).
The saying about alms is from Tobit, a book in the Catholic Bible (the Council of Trent lists it). Polycarp states it without a formula, as a truth the church knew.

views.H: The Latin version survives within the Latin collection of Ignatius's letters (Lake's introduction). It is the only witness for 10:1-12:3, the end of 13:2 and 14:1, so every word of these chapters is one step removed from Polycarp.
views.N: 1 Peter again: 3:8 and 2:17 (love of the brothers), 5:5 (submit to one another), 2:12 (good conduct among the Gentiles); and Isaiah 52:5 in the Greek form Paul quotes in Romans 2:24.
views.C: Almsgiving is urged without hesitation. How giving to the poor relates to forgiveness of sins is a point where today's churches differ; the site's cards at Tobit 4 and Proverbs 16 set out the views. Polycarp here simply calls the church to give, and soon.

echoes: Colossians 1:23; 1 Corinthians 15:58; 1 Peter 3:8; 1 Peter 2:17; John 13:34; Tobit 4:10; Tobit 12:9; 1 Peter 5:5; Ephesians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:12; Isaiah 52:5; Romans 2:24; Matthew 18:7

settings.what: Exhortation: firm faith, mutual love, alms and good conduct
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: After the examples of the martyrs; the text survives only in Latin
settings.why: To turn endurance into daily life: love in the church, quick generosity, and conduct that does not shame Christ among the city's pagans.

title: Valens
sum: Polycarp is deeply grieved over Valens, once an elder at Philippi, who 'understands so little of the place he was given' (11:1). Keep away from greed, he warns: the greedy man is stained with idolatry and judged with the Gentiles, and the saints are to judge the world (11:2). He has heard nothing like it of the Philippians themselves, Paul's own church (11:3). He prays for Valens and his wife to receive true repentance, and tells the church not to treat them as enemies but to call them back as wandering members of the body (11:4).
This is the only crisis the letter names, and it explains the repeated warnings about the love of money in chapters 2-6.

views.H: Valens is known only from this chapter. Harrison named chapters 1-12 the 'Crisis Letter' (1936; reply of 1948). The Latin of 11:3 is obscure, and Lake suggests the lost Greek meant 'who were his letters in the beginning' (2 Corinthians 3:2).
views.N: Ephesians 5:5 and Colossians 3:5 (greed is idolatry), Jeremiah 5:4, 1 Corinthians 6:2 ('as Paul teaches'), 2 Thessalonians 1:4 (boasting among the churches), 2 Timothy 2:25 and 2 Thessalonians 3:15 (repentance, not enmity).
views.C: Polycarp's handling of Valens is a model of church discipline that is firm about the sin and gentle with the sinner: grief, warning, prayer for repentance, and restoration as a member of the body. How churches today should treat an unrepentant member is the question of the site's cards at 2 Thessalonians 3, 1 Corinthians 5 and Matthew 18.

echoes: Colossians 3:5; Ephesians 5:5; Jeremiah 5:4; 1 Corinthians 6:2; Philippians 1:3-11; Philippians 4:15; 2 Corinthians 3:2; 2 Thessalonians 1:4; 2 Timothy 2:25; 2 Thessalonians 3:15; 1 Corinthians 12:26

settings.what: The case of Valens, the fallen elder
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: After an elder of Philippi and his wife had fallen into greed; the text survives only in Latin
settings.why: To grieve with the church, to name the sin and its seriousness, and above all to stop the Philippians from treating Valens and his wife as enemies. Knowing that the whole letter leads up to this case changes how its earlier warnings read.

title: Be angry, but do not sin
sum: Polycarp trusts that the Philippians know the sacred writings better than he does, but reminds them, 'as it is said in these Scriptures', 'Be angry, but do not sin', and 'Do not let the sun set on your anger' (12:1). He prays that God the Father and Jesus Christ, 'the eternal high priest', will build them up and give them a share among the saints (12:2), and he asks them to pray for all the saints, for kings and rulers, for persecutors and for the enemies of the cross (12:3).
The words from Ephesians 4:26, possibly called 'Scriptures', make this chapter important for the history of the New Testament canon.

views.H: In Latin only. Lake's footnotes: the compliment of 12:1 may quote the Philippians' own letter, and 'kings' renders the Greek title of the emperor. Some Latin manuscripts lack 'and God' in 12:2 (variant entry).
views.N: Ephesians 4:26 with Psalm 4:4 (Greek Psalm 4:5), Hebrews 6:20 ('high priest forever'), Galatians 1:1, Colossians 1:12, 1 Timothy 2:1-2, Matthew 5:44, Philippians 3:18 and John 15:16. Whether Polycarp calls Ephesians Scripture depends on how far 'these Scriptures' reaches.
views.C: The prayer for emperors and persecutors in 12:3 follows 1 Timothy 2 and Jesus' command. It was asked of a church under a government that could kill its members, as it killed Polycarp himself.

deep.b: The Latin says ut his scripturis dictum est, 'as it is said in these Scriptures', and then quotes two lines that stand together in Ephesians 4:26. The first line is also the Greek Psalm 4 (Psalm 4:4 in the site's numbering), which Paul is quoting. The second is Paul's own. So Polycarp either calls both lines, and so Ephesians, Scripture, or he names the Psalm as Scripture and adds Paul's comment. 2 Peter 3:16 already speaks of Paul's letters beside 'the other Scriptures'. The Latin translator could also have shaped the phrase. The Plain English Translation uses the site's Ephesians 4:26 wording, with a note on the Psalm.

echoes: Psalm 4:4; Ephesians 4:26; 2 Timothy 3:15; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:3; Galatians 1:1; John 20:28; Colossians 1:12; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; Matthew 5:44; Luke 6:27; Philippians 3:18; John 15:16; 1 Timothy 4:15; James 1:4

settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: Answering the Philippians' compliment (Lake: perhaps quoted from their letter)
settings.why: To keep anger from turning into sin. The letter does not say that the church was angry, but the reminder comes straight after the case of Valens (11:4).

settings.what: Prayer and blessing; a call to pray for all
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.why: To bless the church and to widen its prayers to rulers and persecutors, the people most likely to harm it.

title: The letters of Ignatius
sum: Both the Philippians and Ignatius had asked that anyone going to Syria take the Philippians' letter, and Polycarp promises to do it, himself or by an envoy (13:1). As they asked, he sends them the letters of Ignatius that he has, attached to this letter, for their faith and endurance (13:2). The last sentence, in Latin only, asks for any sure news of Ignatius and those with him (13:2).
This chapter is the reason the letter exists: Lake calls it a 'covering letter' for the copies of Ignatius's letters, sent because the Philippians wanted 'to make a collection' of them.

views.H: Eusebius quotes 13:1-2 to show that Polycarp knew Ignatius's letters (Church History 3.36.14-15). Ignatius's own letters confirm the request about Syria (To Polycarp 7-8; To the Smyrnaeans 11). The final question about Ignatius, if he was still alive, is the main argument that chapters 13-14 were written before chapters 1-12 (see chapter 9).
views.C: Collecting, copying and sending a martyr's letters is an early sign of how the churches shared writings they valued. Polycarp's covering letter and Ignatius's letters traveled together in the manuscripts: the Latin of Polycarp survives inside the Latin collection of Ignatius (Lake).

deep.b: Everything depends on the date of Ignatius. Jerome says Ignatius 'was put to death the eleventh year of Trajan' (Lives of Illustrious Men 16). Harrison (1948) put the Covering Note and the death of Ignatius 'probably towards the end of Trajan's reign, but possibly in the early years of Hadrian', within two or three years of AD 117, and the Crisis Letter in 135-137. The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that anyone who read 7:1 as aimed at Marcion had either to reject the letter or bring its date, 'and the date of St. Ignatius' martyrdom', down 'to A.D. 130-140 when Marcion was prominent'. On the one-letter view the whole letter is as early as Ignatius's journey. Lake gives Polycarp's martyrdom 'in all probability' as 23 February 155 but no date for the letter. The site's source entry for the letter says about AD 110-135.

settings.what: Covering note for the letters of Ignatius
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: Sent with copies of Ignatius's letters, after Ignatius had passed through Smyrna and Philippi on his way to Rome
settings.why: To answer the Philippians' requests: to carry their letter to the church at Antioch in Syria, and to send them Ignatius's letters to read. It shows a network of churches writing to one another around a martyr.
views: Chapters 1-14 were written together, soon after Ignatius left; 9:2 counts him among the martyrs in advance (the Catholic Encyclopedia).

Chapter 13 is an early covering note and 1-12 a later 'Crisis Letter' about Valens (P. N. Harrison, 1936). C. J. Cadoux and C. H. Dodd also took it as two letters, the second written soon after the first (Harrison's reply, 1948).

title: Farewell
sum: Polycarp has written by the hand of Crescens, whom he commends again for his blameless life, and he commends Crescens's sister, who will come later. 'Farewell in the Lord Jesus Christ, in grace, with all who are yours. Amen' (14:1). The chapter survives only in Latin.

views.C: Letters traveled with trusted carriers, who were commended in them, as Paul commended Phoebe (Romans 16:1-2). A woman traveling between churches is commended in the same breath as her brother.

settings.what: Commendation of the letter carrier, and farewell
settings.by: Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, as Eusebius and Jerome call him, with the elders of his church (1:0)
settings.when: At the close of the letter; the text survives only in Latin
settings.why: To make sure the Philippians receive Crescens and, later, his sister, as trusted members of another church.
